statement: Car A leaves a town at 9:00 at 60 km/h. Car B leaves the same town at 9:30 along the same road at 80 km/h. Car C leaves the town at 10:00 along the same road at a steady speed and passes A and B at exactly the same moment. What is the speed of car C, in km/h?

choices.misconception: I found where B catches A, 120 km away at 11:00, but divided by the 2 hours since 9:00 instead of C's 1 hour.
I took the average of the speeds of A and B.
I found where B catches A, 120 km away, but divided by the 1.5 hours since 9:30 instead of C's 1 hour.
I assumed the speeds go up by 20 km/h each time a car leaves later.

hints: When can one car pass two others at the same moment?
C can only pass A and B together when A and B are side by side, which is when B catches A. Find that time and place, then the speed C needs to get there.
B catches A when $80(t - \frac{1}{2}) = 60t$, with $t$ in hours after 9:00. That gives $t = 2$, at 11:00, 120 km from town.

solutions.reliable: C passes both cars at once only if A and B are at the same place then, so it happens when B catches A. Measuring $t$ in hours after 9:00: $60t = 80(t - \frac{1}{2})$ gives $20t = 40$, so $t = 2$: at 11:00, 120 km from the town. C leaves at 10:00, so it covers 120 km in 1 hour: 120 km/h. The transferable idea: in chase problems, first find what has to be true at the key moment, then use distance = speed $\times$ time.
solutions.elegant: At 9:30 A is 30 km ahead of B and B gains 20 km each hour, so B catches A 1.5 hours later, at 11:00, after A has driven 2 hours, 120 km. C needs 120 km in 1 hour.

whyOnTest: Rate problems reward reading for the hidden condition: passing two cars at once forces those cars to be together, then the arithmetic is short.
